title: What Compression Keeps
dek: Compression keeps every bit of information and spends fewer bits on it. Compaction keeps only the present and lets the past go. This is a long explainer of the first — entropy, models and coders, the LZ family, the codecs that matter in October 2026, the prediction contests at the frontier, lossy coding, compression on the wire and as an attack — and of the second in all its senses, from LSM trees and Kafka to garbage collectors, git and an agent's context window, measured where a machine can measure it, and compared side by side.
byline: 9 October 2026 · Synthesised from the original papers, RFCs, release notes and maintainers' own words; sizes and ratios measured on this machine; the XO examples are read from its tree
description: How compression works — entropy, modelling and coding, LZ dictionaries, the 2026 codecs, prediction, lossy coding, HTTP and security — and how it differs from compaction in storage engines, logs, garbage collectors, git and LLM agent context.
og_description: Compression keeps all the information in fewer bits; compaction keeps only the present. Shannon to zstd and OpenZL, Hutter Prize 2026, RFC 9842 dictionary transport, BREACH and the xz backdoor — then LSM, Kafka, VACUUM, GC, git gc and agent context compaction, side by side.
twitter_description: Compression keeps everything in fewer bits. Compaction keeps only the present. A long explainer of both, measured, and the difference that matters.
badges_callout:
How to read the badges

from the paper marks a result taken from the original paper or report (Shannon 1948, Huffman 1952, the Bigtable and Raft papers, and so on). from the spec marks text from an RFC or a format specification. from the docs marks a project's own documentation, release notes, issue tracker, CVE record or a maintainer's words. from the tree marks something read from the XO source trees on this machine, with its path and line numbers. measured here marks a result produced by _compute.py beside this page on one shared 2-CPU Linux machine; sizes and ratios are exact, timings are tiers. reconstruction marks a judgement or mechanism I have worked out rather than read.

sections.title: Fewer bits, or fewer things
sections.brief: Thesis: compression and compaction are two different promises. Compression keeps all the information and spends fewer bits on it; lossless compression is reversible, lossy compression keeps what a perceptual model says matters. Compaction keeps only what a reader can still observe — the current state — and rewrites it densely; superseded versions, tombstones past their grace period, dead tuples and unreachable objects are gone and cannot come back. The words have traded places before (compaction.md section A: 1970s 'data compaction' papers meant compression; the UNIX `compact` utility was an adaptive-Huffman compressor). Show the measured three-treatments result as the hook: the same key-value update log, (a) compressed with zstd, (b) compacted to the last value per key, (c) compacted then compressed — sizes from _numbers.json → treatments, and which of the three can reproduce the history. 'The answer, up front' (h3, reconstruction): use compression when you must keep every byte or every frame and want it smaller (storage, transfer); use compaction when old versions have no reader (LSM stores, Kafka changelogs, VACUUM, GC, agent context); most storage engines do both in one pass, and the order matters (compact first, then compress what is left). Point to the companion practical post ../what-each-file-wants/ for per-format recipes and to ../where-the-json-lives/ for storage engines.
figures: fig-two-pipelines · two promises (SVG, wide) · top lane, compression: bytes -> model -> entropy coder -> fewer bits -> decoder -> the same bytes (lossless) or a perceptually close copy (lossy); bottom lane, compaction: a log of versions and tombstones -> merge -> only the live state, history dropped (dashed purple = state discarded). Label what each keeps and what each cannot undo.

sections.title: Information is surprise
sections.brief: Shannon 1948 (theory.md section A; quote verbatim from the primary PDF): entropy H = −Σ p log p (Theorem 2, and his remark that the axioms are 'in no way necessary'), typical sequences and the 2^(HN) picture (Theorems 3–4), the source coding theorem (Theorem 9). Bits per symbol as the unit; a worked example with a biased coin and with English letters (only if in the dossier). Measured: empirical order-0 entropy of a few corpora on this machine vs what gzip/zstd/xz achieve (_numbers.json → entropy), showing that real compressors beat order-0 entropy because they model context — entropy is relative to a model. Kolmogorov complexity (Kolmogorov 1965, Problems of Information Transmission; theory.md section D): the shortest program; uncomputable. The counting argument (comp.compression FAQ §9.2 verbatim, theory.md section C): no lossless compressor shrinks every input; Mahoney: at most 2^(m−n) of n-bit strings compress to m bits, fewer than 0.4% compress by even one byte; DEFLATE's worst case 5 bytes per 32 KiB block (RFC 1951 §1.1). Measured: random bytes through gzip/zstd/xz/brotli expand by a few bytes (_numbers.json → random). FLAC on random data 107.8% (theory.md F28 corrected).
figures: fig-entropy · entropy of a biased coin and where real files sit (SVG) · the binary entropy curve H(p); beside it, measured bits per byte for the corpora: order-0 entropy vs gzip vs zstd vs xz from _numbers.json → entropy.
fig-pigeonhole · why nothing shrinks everything (SVG) · 2^n inputs of n bits mapping into the 2^n − 1 shorter strings; the 0.4% bound; measured overhead on random input per codec.

sections.title: A model and a coder
sections.brief: Every compressor is a model that predicts and a coder that spends bits on the prediction's surprise (Rissanen & Langdon 1981; Witten, Neal & Cleary 1987 say the separation 'costs nothing' with arithmetic coding — theory.md section E). Coders: Huffman 1952 (paper, venue; whole-bit codes, optimal among prefix codes; the cost when a probability is far from a power of 1/2); arithmetic coding (Elias early 1960s, Rissanen and Pasco 1976, the 1987 CACM implementation), range coding (Martin 1979, described by RFC 6716 and libaom as a rediscovery of Pasco 1976); ANS (Duda arXiv 0902.0271 and 1311.2540): tANS/FSE in zstd (RFC 8878 §4.1) and LZFSE, rANS in JPEG XL (which may use prefix codes instead per stream) and Draco; AV1 does NOT use ANS — its spec uses adaptive-CDF arithmetic coding and libaom's entdec.c is a range decoder (myth, theory.md). Google's ANS patent application abandoned (F75). Worked example: the same short message coded with Huffman vs arithmetic, bits counted (compute in the harness or by hand, mark which). CABAC in H.264 as adaptive binary arithmetic coding (media.md section 1).
figures: fig-arith · arithmetic coding narrows an interval (SVG, wide) · a three-symbol alphabet with probabilities, the interval subdivided for a 4-symbol message, final interval width = product of probabilities, bits ≈ −log2(width); compared with the Huffman code lengths for the same message.

fig-coders · which coder ships where (stack rows) · Huffman (DEFLATE, JPEG baseline, zstd literals), arithmetic/range (H.264 CABAC, AV1, LZMA's range coder, Opus), tANS/FSE (zstd, LZFSE), rANS (JPEG XL option, Draco); each with its source.

sections.title: Saying it again, by reference
sections.brief: The other half of practical compression is modelling repetition. LZ77 (Ziv & Lempel 1977, IEEE Trans. IT) — a sliding window and (distance, length) back-references; LZ78 (1978) — an explicit dictionary; LZSS (Storer & Szymanski 1982); LZW (Welch 1984) and the Unisys patent US 4,558,302 (filed 1983-06-20, granted 1985-12-10, expiries 2003–2004 per Unisys's archived notice), the GIF controversy and the first PNG draft (4 Jan 1995) (theory.md sections I, J; note the unresolved 24 vs 28 Dec 1994 date conflict — do not state either as fact unless the dossier resolves it). BWT (Burrows & Wheeler 1994, DEC SRC report 124) and bzip2; PPM (Cleary & Witten 1984); context mixing — PAQ, cmix. Measured: an LZ77 parse of a short real string shown as literals and matches (generate in the harness: _numbers.json → lz_demo), and the effect of window size (zstd --long / window log) on a corpus with long-distance repeats (_numbers.json → window). Pre-shared dictionaries as 'repetition you already sent': zstd --train, Brotli's built-in 122,784-byte dictionary (RFC 7932 Appendix A; decoded: 13,504 words, mostly multilingual web text, only ~1k HTML/CSS/JS fragments — codecs.md).
figures: fig-lz77 · a sliding window turns repeats into pointers (SVG, wide, measured) · a real short string from the harness with literals and (distance, length) matches drawn as arcs back into the window; counts of literal vs matched bytes.
fig-window · reach matters (SVG, measured) · ratio vs window size (zstd window log) on a corpus with long-range repetition, from _numbers.json → window.

sections.title: The codecs that matter in 2026
sections.brief: A ledger of the general-purpose lossless codecs as of 9 October 2026 (codecs.md sections 0–8; every version and date from the dossier's verified snapshot): DEFLATE (RFC 1951), zlib (RFC 1950), gzip (RFC 1952); zlib 1.3.2, zlib-ng 2.3.3, libdeflate 1.26, Zopfli, GNU gzip 1.15 (2026-09-20). Brotli (RFC 7932, v1.2.0 2025-10-27; CLI default quality 11 vs zstd's level 3 — 'default vs default' comparisons mislead; the '20–26% better than gzip' line is a misattribution of a claim against Zopfli). Zstandard (RFC 8878 is Informational; RFC 8478 first registered application/zstd; v1.5.7 2025-02-19 still latest; levels negative to 22, --ultra, --long; dictionaries). LZ4 1.10.0, Snappy 1.3.1, LZFSE; xz/LZMA2 (XZ Utils 5.8.4), 7-Zip 26.04, bzip2 1.0.8 (1.1.0 unreleased); OpenZL (Meta, 2025-10-06, BSD, format-aware graph of transforms, falls back to zstd, Meta's SAO claim x2.06 vs zstd -3 x1.31 and xz -9 x1.64; v0.3.0 2026-09-29). Measured on this machine: the speed/ratio frontier on a standard-ish mixed corpus (the harness should use a reproducible public corpus such as Silesia if downloadable, or a documented local mix) — compression and decompression speed tiers and exact ratios per codec and level (_numbers.json → frontier). Cite lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P) as the neutral published table, noting its ratio convention (% of original) vs zstd/LZ4 READMEs (original/compressed). Decompression asymmetry: most codecs decode far faster than they encode.
figures: fig-frontier · the speed–ratio frontier (SVG chart, wide, measured) · x = compression speed (log), y = ratio, one point per codec/level from _numbers.json → frontier, the Pareto frontier drawn; a second marker for decompression speed; caption: tiers, one contended machine.

sections.title: Compression is prediction
sections.brief: The frontier of lossless compression is a prediction contest. Hutter Prize (page modified 30 Sep 2026): record fx2-cmix-T by Vladimir Ivanov, 100,424,672 bytes (24 Jul 2026; 7.46% improvement; €37,300), a 6M-parameter transformer pretrained on enwik9 with 8 RTX 5090s; before it cmix-obias, cmix-lex, fx2-cmix (110,793,128, Sep 2024) — the record changed three times in 2026. LTCB (5 Oct 2026): top five cmix-derived transformers, led by cmix-neif 1.0 at 91,913,343 bytes; rata-cmix is explicitly not a Hutter candidate; NNCP v3.3 best 106,632,363 (0.853 bpb); paq8px v217. Mind the conventions: LTCB prints compressed/original, Hutter original/compressed, and they count decompressor size differently (theory.md myths). 'Language Modeling Is Compression' (Delétang et al., ICLR 2024): Chinchilla 70B 43.4% on ImageNet and 16.4% on LibriSpeech vs PNG 58.5% and FLAC 30.3%, explicitly excluding model size; counting parameters, ~14,048% on 1 GB; and the paper's own Table 1 reports 48.0%/21.0% (theory.md, verified). So 'LLMs beat PNG' is true only with the weights excluded. What this means for agents: a model's weights are a dictionary the size of the internet; the relevant cost is the shared context both ends already hold (reconstruction). Link to the context-compaction section.
figures: fig-hutter · enwik9 records, 2006–2026 (SVG timeline, measured from sources) · Hutter Prize record sizes over time with the 2026 steps; LTCB's best entry as a separate marker; axis in bytes with both ratio conventions noted.

sections.title: Throwing away what nobody sees
sections.brief: Lossy compression changes the question from 'how few bits' to 'how few bits for this much distortion': rate–distortion theory (Shannon 1948 §28 Theorem 21; Shannon 1959 R(d) convex and decreasing — theory.md section B). The pipeline: transform (DCT, Ahmed/Natarajan/Rao 1974; JPEG T.81's 8×8 FDCT → quantizer → entropy coder), quantization tables 'based on psychovisual thresholding' and examples only (T.81 Annex K), psychoacoustic masking (Opus RFC 6716), rate control (VBR/CBR, bit reservoir). Standards specify the decoder, not the encoder (AV1 spec: the encoding process is not specified). Measuring loss: PSNR, SSIM (2004), VMAF (Netflix 2016: PSNR 'does not consistently reflect human perception', the 31 vs 34 dB example), VMAF v1 models (June 2026), SSIMULACRA 2, XPSNR; BD-rate (draft-ietf-netvc-testing-09 §4.2). Generation loss (JPEG XL paper 2025). Keep this section conceptual; the practical recipes and measurements for images, audio and video belong to ../what-each-file-wants/ — link to it.
figures: fig-transform · a transform coder in four steps (SVG, wide) · block → DCT coefficients → quantization (most high-frequency coefficients become zero) → entropy coding; with a small numeric 8×8 example if the harness provides one (_numbers.json → dct_demo), else marked reconstruction.

sections.title: Compression on the wire
sections.brief: HTTP is where most people meet compression. Content-Encoding vs Transfer-Encoding; Accept-Encoding negotiation; br, gzip, zstd. Support: Content-Encoding zstd in Chrome 123 (2024-03-19), Firefox 126 (2024-05-14), Safari 26.3 partial on desktop (requires macOS 26.3 Tahoe; caniuse 'partial') — codecs.md F58 correction; Chrome advertises br and zstd only over HTTPS or localhost. RFC 9659 (Sept 2024) makes an 8 MB window a MUST for HTTP zstd, so --long and large-window ultra levels are invalid on the wire. Compression Dictionary Transport is RFC 9842 (Standards Track, Sept 2025) with RFC 9841 Shared Brotli: Use-As-Dictionary, Available-Dictionary (SHA-256), Dictionary-ID; dcb and dcz encodings and their headers/windows; Chrome 130 on by default; Firefox behind a pref (the 'Firefox 147 shipped it' claim is unsupported). CDNs: Cloudflare defaults (zstd on Free, Brotli on Pro/Business, gzip on Enterprise; minimum sizes 48/50 bytes); nginx gzip_min_length 20 and gzips only text/html by default; Vercel's docs list gzip and Brotli only and say 'brotli' where the token is 'br'; live probes returned br for 'zstd, br, gzip' and nothing for 'zstd' alone (codecs.md/inventory.md). Note the inventory finding that this site's own Vercel project is currently not serving (deployments in ERROR) — mention only as 'at the time of writing, probes were made against www.quirq.ai and vercel.com' exactly as the dossier records; do not speculate. Measured: response sizes for a real page (this site's what-the-parser-hears/index.html, 0.4 MiB) under gzip -6/-9, br 5/11, zstd 3/19, and with a dictionary built from where-the-json-lives/index.html (_numbers.json → wire).

sections.title: When compression is the attack
sections.brief: Compression leaks and compression explodes. Side channels: CRIME (2012), BREACH (2013; CVE-2013-3587 published by NVD 2020-02-21 — RFC 7457 §2.6 still says unallocated, which is outdated), HEIST — mechanism: the attacker injects guesses next to a secret and watches the compressed length; mitigations (separate secrets from reflected input, masking tokens per request, length padding). Dictionary transport's privacy considerations (RFC 9842 §10, codecs.md section 10). Decompression bombs: Fifield 2019 'A better zip bomb' (sizes from the dossier), library limits (Python zlib max_length, zipfile, Pillow MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS), measured: a small zstd/gzip bomb ratio produced and safely bounded in the harness (_numbers.json → bombs). Supply chain: the xz backdoor CVE-2024-3094 (CVSS 10.0): only the 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 tarballs; trigger build-to-host.m4 only in tarballs; payload in test files in git; x86-64 Linux, gcc + GNU ld, deb/rpm builds; IFUNC resolvers and RSA_public_decrypt in sshd via libsystemd; Freund's timings 0.299 s → 0.807 s (codecs.md F95 corrected — quote with the ellipsis); 5.6.2 (2024-05-29) removed it. The YAML alias bomb in ../what-the-parser-hears/ is the same family as a decompression bomb — link.
figures: fig-breach · how a length leaks a secret (SVG, wide) · a response containing a secret token and attacker-reflected input; when the guess matches, LZ77 turns it into a back-reference and the compressed response is shorter; three guesses with their measured compressed lengths from _numbers.json → oracle (computed with zlib in the harness on a synthetic page).
fig-hazard-ledger · compression incidents and their fixes (HTML table) · CRIME, BREACH, HEIST, zip bombs, CVE-2024-3094: year, mechanism, what changed afterwards.

sections.title: Compaction: keeping only the present
sections.brief: Compaction in every sense, each with what it keeps, what it drops, what triggers it and what it costs (compaction.md sections B–I, L). Invariants as the sources state them: SQLite VACUUM INTO 'the same logical content'; Delta OPTIMIZE 'a read before and after ... has the same results'; Kafka keeps 'at least the final state of all records' with offsets and order unchanged; Cassandra keeps 'the most up-to-date version (by timestamp)'; physical identity not preserved (SQLite ROWIDs may change; GC moves objects). LSM trees: O'Neil 1996 'rolling merge' (the paper never says compaction; 'delete node entries' as ancestors of tombstones); Bigtable 2006 §5.4 minor, merging and major compactions (quote; the 10-to-1 figure only with its conditions — F17 correction); RocksDB leveled vs universal (up to 2× space), write/read/space amplification and the RUM conjecture (Athanassoulis et al. EDBT 2016); RocksDB default compression is LZ4 since 11.5.0 (F33 correction), ZSTD recommended for bottommost, per-SST dictionaries; Cassandra STCS/LCS/TWCS/UCS (UCS recommended; 5.0.9 latest GA; 6.0 alpha only), tombstones and gc_grace_seconds. Kafka: cleanup.policy=compact, 'at least the last known value', min.cleanable.dirty.ratio 0.5 so duplicates can be half the log; batch compression codecs are a separate setting. Databases: PostgreSQL VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL (exclusive lock, full rewrite; autovacuum never issues FULL), PG 19 beta REPACK (CONCURRENTLY); SQLite VACUUM (up to 2×) and auto_vacuum; MongoDB compact / autoCompact (8.0); etcd compaction (drops history) vs defrag (returns space). Data lakes: Iceberg rewrite_data_files, Delta OPTIMIZE — which also re-encode and recompress. Memory: mark-compact GC, V8 Orinoco, G1/ZGC relocation; Linux kcompactd for huge pages. File systems: LFS cleaning (Rosenblum & Ousterhout 1991), F2FS GC, defrag. Git gc/repack: loose objects into packs, delta compression + zlib, prune — does both. Raft §7 log compaction via snapshots (quote). Event stores and CRDTs (Yjs GC) briefly. Measured: a SQLite file before and after deletes and after VACUUM; a mini key-value log compacted (last value per key) with its amplification; a git repo before and after gc (_numbers.json → compaction).

sections.title: Compacting a conversation
sections.brief: The newest sense, and the one that matters most to agent builders: compacting an LLM agent's context window. It is lossy semantic compression plus eviction, with no exact invariant (compaction.md section J). Claude Code: /compact and auto-compaction (about 967K tokens on 1M-window models per the docs; early instructions 'may be lost'; path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md files are summarised away but 'reloaded on demand' — F142 correction; quote the table rows). Claude API: threshold compaction (compact-2026-01-12 / compact_20260112, default trigger 150K, minimum 50K), on-demand compaction (beta header compact-2026-09-04, top-level compaction parameter), context editing (context-management-2025-06-27); images, documents and fetched URLs in the summarised range 'are gone' (F153). OpenAI: /responses/compact (11 Dec 2025), server-side compaction (10 Feb 2026); the compaction item is encrypted and 'not intended to be human-interpretable' (F158); Codex's compaction prompt 'CONTEXT CHECKPOINT COMPACTION … handoff summary'. Anthropic itself describes compaction as 'summarize and compress' (F6). Read the writings repo's own ../claude-code-session/ and ../codex-session/ posts and quote what they say about compaction (paths). In the XO tree: mindwalk detects compaction events (Claude Code system subtype containing 'compact', Codex context_compacted, pi compaction/branch) and xo-space adapters hard-code time_compacted/time_compacting to None (inventory.md section 16; cite path:line). Compare with the storage senses: a storage compaction preserves the logical state exactly; a context compaction preserves only what the summariser judged relevant — which is why it is the one compaction that needs a human-readable audit trail (reconstruction). Measured (optional if the harness can do it without an API): token counts are not measured here; do not invent any.
figures: fig-context · a context window before and after compaction (SVG, wide) · turns, tool results and files filling the window; at the threshold, a summary block replaces the older range; what survives (summary, recent turns, reloaded CLAUDE.md), what is gone (images, documents, fetched URLs in the summarised range); dashed purple for discarded state.

sections.title: Compression and compaction, side by side
sections.brief: The comparison the reader came for. Definitions (reconstruction refined from compaction.md section N): compression changes the encoding — the same data in fewer bits, judged by ratio, speed and (if lossy) distortion; lossless compression is reversible. Compaction rewrites the live data densely and drops what no reader can observe any more — judged by write, read and space amplification and pauses — and cannot be undone. Two refinements from the sources: some compactions discard nothing (defragmentation, Linux memory compaction, GC moving live objects), so the defining property is 'reorganise for the present', with discarding as the common case; and LLM context compaction is a third kind: lossy, semantic, irreversible. Where they meet: RocksDB, Cassandra ('the compression will not be modified until the table is compacted'), data-lake OPTIMIZE and git gc apply or re-apply compression during compaction; Kafka, Bigtable and MongoDB keep them as separate settings. Order matters: compact then compress (measured in the three-treatments figure). Myths (compaction.md myths, each with its source): compaction and compression are the same thing; Kafka compaction keeps only the latest value; deleting data frees disk space (etcd: 'deleting application data does not reclaim the space on disk'); compaction always shrinks storage (it often needs up to 2× first); VACUUM FULL is the normal bloat fix. 'Compact JSON' (minification) sits between: it removes redundant bytes like compression, irreversibly like compaction (formatting is lost), and gzip makes most of it moot (measured: pretty vs minified, raw and compressed, _numbers.json → minify). End with a decision rule paragraph (reconstruction).
